theorySlides.title: Headings 📰
theorySlides.content:
HTML has 6 heading levels, from h1 (largest) to h6 (smallest):

<h1> - Main heading
<h2> - Section heading
<h3> - Subsection
<h4>, <h5>, <h6> - Smaller headings

Use headings to organize your content logically!

theorySlides.title: What is CSS? 🎨
theorySlides.content:
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML elements look.

If HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin, clothes, and makeup!

With CSS you control:
• Colors
• Fonts
• Spacing
• Layout
• Animations

questions.explanation: CSS = Cascading Style Sheets.

questions.question: Which is the best way to add CSS?
questions.explanation: External CSS files are best for maintainability and reusability.

questions.question: What is CSS specificity?
options: The priority system for conflicting styles
questions.explanation: CSS specificity determines which style rules apply when multiple rules target the same element. Inline > ID > Class > Element.

questions.question: Which CSS selector has the highest specificity?
questions.explanation: Inline styles have the highest specificity, followed by IDs, classes, and element selectors.

questions.question: What does the "Cascading" in CSS mean?
options: Styles cascade from parent to child elements
questions.explanation: Cascading refers to how styles from multiple sources combine, inherit from parent to child, and override each other based on specificity.

theorySlides.title: The Box Model 📦
theorySlides.content:
Every HTML element is a box! The box model consists of:

• Content - The actual text/image
• Padding - Space around content
• Border - Line around padding
• Margin - Space outside border

theorySlides.title: Padding
theorySlides.content: Padding creates space inside the element, between content and border.

theorySlides.title: Margin
theorySlides.content: Margin creates space outside the element, separating it from other elements.

theorySlides.title: Border
theorySlides.content: Borders wrap around padding and content.

questions.question: What does padding affect?
questions.explanation: Padding creates space inside the element, between content and border.

questions.question: How do you center an element horizontally with margin?
questions.explanation: margin: 0 auto; sets top/bottom to 0 and left/right to auto, centering the element.

questions.question: What is the default box-sizing value?
questions.explanation: By default, box-sizing is content-box, where width/height only apply to content. border-box includes padding and border in the dimensions.

questions.question: What happens when you set box-sizing: border-box?
options: Padding and border are included in the element's width/height
questions.explanation: border-box makes width/height include padding and border, making sizing more predictable.

questions.question: What is margin collapse?
options: When vertical margins between elements combine into one
questions.explanation: Margin collapse occurs when vertical margins of adjacent elements overlap, and the larger margin wins.

lessons.description: Create flexible layouts with CSS Flexbox

theorySlides.title: What is Flexbox? 🎯
theorySlides.content:
Flexbox is a powerful layout system that makes it easy to:

• Align items horizontally or vertically
• Distribute space between items
• Create responsive layouts
• Center content perfectly

theorySlides.title: Flex Container
theorySlides.content: Enable flexbox by setting display: flex on the parent container.

theorySlides.title: justify-content
theorySlides.content: Controls alignment along the main axis (horizontal by default).

theorySlides.title: Flex Items
theorySlides.content: Control how individual items grow, shrink, or align.

questions.question: How do you enable Flexbox?
questions.explanation: Set display: flex on the container element to enable Flexbox.

questions.question: Which property centers items horizontally in a flex row?
questions.explanation: justify-content controls alignment along the main axis (horizontal in row direction).

questions.question: What does flex-direction: column do?
questions.explanation: flex-direction: column changes the main axis to vertical, making items stack from top to bottom.

questions.question: What does flex: 1 do to a flex item?
options: Makes it grow to fill available space
questions.explanation: flex: 1 makes the item grow to fill available space, with a flex-grow factor of 1.

questions.question: When would you use flex-wrap: wrap?
options: To allow items to wrap to next line when container is too small
questions.explanation: flex-wrap: wrap allows flex items to wrap to multiple lines instead of shrinking or overflowing.

theorySlides.title: What is CSS Grid? 📐
theorySlides.content:
CSS Grid is perfect for 2D layouts with rows AND columns.

Use cases:
• Page layouts
• Image galleries
• Card grids
• Dashboard layouts

theorySlides.title: Grid Container
theorySlides.content: Enable grid and define columns and rows.

theorySlides.title: Grid Units
theorySlides.content: Different ways to size grid tracks.

theorySlides.title: Placing Items
theorySlides.content: Control where items appear in the grid.

questions.question: What does "1fr" mean in CSS Grid?
questions.explanation: fr is a fractional unit that divides available space proportionally.

questions.question: How do you create 4 equal columns?
questions.explanation: repeat(4, 1fr) creates 4 columns, each taking 1 fraction of space.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the gap property in Grid?
questions.explanation: The gap property (or grid-gap) sets spacing between rows and columns in a grid layout.

questions.question: What does grid-column: 1 / 3 mean?
options: Item spans from column line 1 to 3
questions.explanation: grid-column: 1 / 3 makes the item span from grid line 1 to line 3, covering 2 columns.

questions.question: When should you use Grid instead of Flexbox?
options: For complex 2D layouts with rows AND columns
questions.explanation: Use Grid for 2D layouts where you need control over both rows and columns. Use Flexbox for simpler 1D layouts.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.description: Make your websites work on all screen sizes

theorySlides.title: Why Responsive? 📱
theorySlides.content:
Users browse on many devices:

• Desktop computers (1920px+)
• Laptops (1024-1920px)
• Tablets (768-1024px)
• Phones (320-768px)

Your design must adapt to all of them!

theorySlides.title: Viewport Meta Tag
theorySlides.content: Essential for mobile browsers to render correctly.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
<!-- In your HTML <head> -->
<meta name="viewport" 
      content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

theorySlides.title: Media Queries
theorySlides.content: Apply different styles based on screen size.

theorySlides.title: Mobile-First Approach
theorySlides.content: Start with mobile styles, then add complexity for larger screens.

questions.question: What does the viewport meta tag do?
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers how to render the page width.

questions.question: What is the mobile-first approach?
options: Start with mobile, add for larger screens
questions.explanation: Mobile-first means writing base styles for mobile, then using media queries to enhance for larger screens.

questions.question: What does min-width in a media query mean?
options: Applies styles when screen is AT LEAST this wide
questions.explanation: @media (min-width: 768px) means "apply these styles when the viewport is 768px or wider".

questions.question: What are common responsive breakpoints?
questions.explanation: Common breakpoints target mobile (~480px), tablet (~768px), and desktop (~1024px+) devices.

questions.question: Why use relative units (%, em, rem) instead of pixels for responsive design?
options: They adapt better to different screen sizes and user preferences
questions.explanation: Relative units scale proportionally and respect user accessibility settings, making designs more flexible and accessible.

lessons.title: CSS Transitions & Animations
lessons.description: Add motion and interactivity to your designs

theorySlides.title: CSS Transitions ✨
theorySlides.content:
Transitions smoothly animate changes between two states.

Use for:
• Hover effects
• Focus states
• Color changes
• Size changes

theorySlides.title: Transition Properties
theorySlides.content: Control what animates and how.

theorySlides.title: CSS Animations
theorySlides.content: For more complex, multi-step animations, use @keyframes.

theorySlides.title: Animation Properties
theorySlides.content: Fine-tune your animations.

questions.question: What is the difference between transition and animation?
options: Transition needs 2 states, animation uses keyframes
questions.explanation: Transitions animate between two states, while animations use @keyframes for complex multi-step sequences.

questions.question: What does "infinite" do in animation-iteration-count?
questions.explanation: infinite makes the animation repeat indefinitely.

questions.question: What is the purpose of animation-timing-function?
options: Controls the speed curve of the animation
questions.explanation: animation-timing-function (ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out, etc.) controls how the animation progresses over time.

questions.question: When should you use transitions vs animations?
options: Transitions for simple 2-state changes, animations for complex sequences
questions.explanation: Use transitions for simple state changes (hover effects). Use @keyframes animations for multi-step, complex motion.

questions.question: What does animation-fill-mode: forwards do?
options: Keeps the final animation state after completion
questions.explanation: forwards makes the element retain the styles from the last keyframe after the animation completes.
